claim: Mimivirus is the prototype of the Mimiviridae family of giant dsDNA viruses.
source: Mimivirus is the prototype of the Mimiviridae family of giant dsDNA viruses.
evidence: This is a definitional statement establishing mimivirus as the prototype of its viral family, representing established scientific knowledge in the field.

claim: The mimivirus genome is 1.2 Mb in size.
source: Little is known about the organization of the 1.2 Mb genome inside the membrane-limited nucleoid filling the ~0.5 µm icosahedral capsids.
evidence: The genome size is stated as a known fact in the abstract and is consistent with published data on mimivirus.

claim: The mimivirus genome is encased in a ~30-nm diameter helical protein shell.
source: Cryo-electron microscopy, cryo-electron tomography, and proteomics revealed that it is encased into a ~30-nm diameter helical protein shell surprisingly composed of two GMC-type oxidoreductases, which also form the glycosylated fibrils decorating the capsid.
evidence: This claim is directly supported by experimental data from cryo-EM, cryo-ET, and proteomics presented in the manuscript.

claim: The helical protein shell encasing the mimivirus genome is composed of two GMC-type oxidoreductases.
source: Cryo-electron microscopy, cryo-electron tomography, and proteomics revealed that it is encased into a ~30-nm diameter helical protein shell surprisingly composed of two GMC-type oxidoreductases, which also form the glycosylated fibrils decorating the capsid.
evidence: This is supported by proteomic analysis identifying qu_946 and qu_143 as the main components of the genomic fiber.

claim: The GMC-type oxidoreductases that form the helical protein shell also form the glycosylated fibrils decorating the capsid.
source: Cryo-electron microscopy, cryo-electron tomography, and proteomics revealed that it is encased into a ~30-nm diameter helical protein shell surprisingly composed of two GMC-type oxidoreductases, which also form the glycosylated fibrils decorating the capsid.
evidence: This is supported by prior knowledge that GMC oxidoreductases compose the fibrils and the current finding that they also compose the genomic fiber.

claim: The mimivirus genome is arranged in 5- or 6-start left-handed super-helices.
source: The genome is arranged in 5- or 6-start left-handed super-helices, with each DNA-strand lining the central channel.
evidence: This is directly supported by cryo-EM structural analysis showing both 5-start and 6-start helical conformations.

claim: Each DNA strand lines the central channel of the helical protein shell.
source: The genome is arranged in 5- or 6-start left-handed super-helices, with each DNA-strand lining the central channel.
evidence: This is supported by cryo-EM and cryo-ET data showing DNA strands lining the interior of the protein shell.

claim: The luminal channel of the nucleoprotein fiber is wide enough to accommodate oxidative stress proteins and RNA polymerase subunits.
source: This luminal channel of the nucleoprotein fiber is wide enough to accommodate oxidative stress proteins and RNA polymerase subunits identified by proteomics.
evidence: This is based on structural measurements from cryo-EM showing a ~9-nm-wide central channel and proteomic identification of these proteins.

claim: The genomic fiber organization represents a strategy for packaging and protecting the genome in a state ready for immediate transcription upon unwinding in the host cytoplasm.
source: Such elegant supramolecular organization would represent a remarkable evolutionary strategy for packaging and protecting the genome, in a state ready for immediate transcription upon unwinding in the host cytoplasm.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation based on the structural findings and the presence of RNA polymerase subunits in the fiber.

claim: The use of the same protein in two unrelated substructures of the virion is unexpected for a giant virus with thousand genes at its disposal.
source: The parsimonious use of the same protein in two unrelated substructures of the virion is unexpected for a giant virus with thousand genes at its disposal.
evidence: This is an interpretive statement based on the finding that GMC oxidoreductases serve dual functions and knowledge about giant virus genome capacity.

claim: Giant viruses were discovered with the isolation of mimivirus (La Scola et al., 2003; Raoult et al., 2004).
source: Acanthamoeba infecting giant viruses were discovered with the isolation of mimivirus (La Scola et al., 2003; Raoult et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citations to the original discovery papers.

claim: Giant viruses represent a highly diverse group of dsDNA viruses infecting unicellular eukaryotes (Abergel et al., 2015).
source: Giant viruses now represent a highly diverse group of dsDNA viruses infecting unicellular eukaryotes (Abergel et al., 2015) which play important roles in the environment (Schulz et al., 2020; Moniruzzaman et al., 2020; Kaneko et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a review article.

claim: Giant viruses play important roles in the environment (Schulz et al., 2020; Moniruzzaman et al., 2020; Kaneko et al., 2021).
source: Giant viruses now represent a highly diverse group of dsDNA viruses infecting unicellular eukaryotes (Abergel et al., 2015) which play important roles in the environment (Schulz et al., 2020; Moniruzzaman et al., 2020; Kaneko et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple research papers.

claim: Giant viruses challenge the canonical definitions of viruses (Forterre, 2010; Claverie and Abergel, 2010).
source: They also challenge the canonical definitions of viruses (Forterre, 2010; Claverie and Abergel, 2010) as they can encode central translation components (Raoult et al., 2004; Abergel et al., 2007) as well as a complete glycosylation machinery (Piacente et al., 2017; Notaro et al., 2021) among other unique features.
evidence: This is supported by citations to papers discussing the implications of giant virus features.

claim: Giant viruses can encode central translation components (Raoult et al., 2004; Abergel et al., 2007).
source: They also challenge the canonical definitions of viruses (Forterre, 2010; Claverie and Abergel, 2010) as they can encode central translation components (Raoult et al., 2004; Abergel et al., 2007) as well as a complete glycosylation machinery (Piacente et al., 2017; Notaro et al., 2021) among other unique features.
evidence: This is supported by citations to papers describing mimivirus genomic features.

claim: Giant viruses can encode a complete glycosylation machinery (Piacente et al., 2017; Notaro et al., 2021).
source: They also challenge the canonical definitions of viruses (Forterre, 2010; Claverie and Abergel, 2010) as they can encode central translation components (Raoult et al., 2004; Abergel et al., 2007) as well as a complete glycosylation machinery (Piacente et al., 2017; Notaro et al., 2021) among other unique features.
evidence: This is supported by citations to papers describing the glycosylation machinery.

claim: Mimivirus has been the most extensively studied giant virus infecting Acanthamoeba (Colson et al., 2017).
source: Mimivirus has been the most extensively studied giant virus infecting Acanthamoeba (Colson et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a review article.

claim: Mimivirus virions are 0.75 µm wide.
source: The virions are 0.75 µm wide and consist of icosahedral capsids of 0.45 µm diameter surrounded by a dense layer of radially arranged fibrils (Raoult et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citation to the original mimivirus discovery paper and represents established knowledge.

claim: Mimivirus virions consist of icosahedral capsids of 0.45 µm diameter surrounded by a dense layer of radially arranged fibrils (Raoult et al., 2004).
source: The virions are 0.75 µm wide and consist of icosahedral capsids of 0.45 µm diameter surrounded by a dense layer of radially arranged fibrils (Raoult et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citation to the original mimivirus discovery paper.

claim: Structural analyses of mimivirus virions have provided insights into the capsid structure (Kuznetsov et al., 2013; Xiao et al., 2009; Klose et al., 2010; Ekeberg et al., 2015; Schrad et al., 2020).
source: Structural analyses of the virions have provided some insights into the capsid structure (Kuznetsov et al., 2013; Xiao et al., 2009; Klose et al., 2010; Ekeberg et al., 2015; Schrad et al., 2020) but given the size of the icosahedral particles (and hence the sample thickness), accessing the internal organization of the core of the virions remains challenging.
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple structural studies.

claim: Accessing the internal organization of the core of mimivirus virions remains challenging due to the size of the icosahedral particles.
source: Structural analyses of the virions have provided some insights into the capsid structure (Kuznetsov et al., 2013; Xiao et al., 2009; Klose et al., 2010; Ekeberg et al., 2015; Schrad et al., 2020) but given the size of the icosahedral particles (and hence the sample thickness), accessing the internal organization of the core of the virions remains challenging.
evidence: This is based on knowledge of technical limitations in structural biology and inference from the literature.

claim: Little is known about the packaging of the 1.2 Mb dsDNA genome (Chelikani et al., 2014).
source: Consequently, little is known about the packaging of the 1.2 Mb dsDNA genome (Chelikani et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation and represents the state of knowledge prior to this study.

claim: A lipid membrane inside the mimivirus capsid delineates an internal compartment (~340 nm in diameter) referred to as the nucleoid.
source: Inside the capsids, a lipid membrane delineates an internal compartment (~340 nm in diameter, Figure 1A, Figure 1—figure supplement 1), referred to as the nucleoid, which contains the viral genome, together with all proteins necessary to initiate the replicative cycle within the host cytoplasm (Schrad et al., 2020; Kuznetsov et al., 2010; Claverie et al., 2009; Arslan et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations and by Figure 1A showing the nucleoid structure.

claim: The nucleoid contains the viral genome together with all proteins necessary to initiate the replicative cycle within the host cytoplasm (Schrad et al., 2020; Kuznetsov et al., 2010; Claverie et al., 2009; Arslan et al., 2011).
source: Inside the capsids, a lipid membrane delineates an internal compartment (~340 nm in diameter, Figure 1A, Figure 1—figure supplement 1), referred to as the nucleoid, which contains the viral genome, together with all proteins necessary to initiate the replicative cycle within the host cytoplasm (Schrad et al., 2020; Kuznetsov et al., 2010; Claverie et al., 2009; Arslan et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior studies.

claim: Acanthamoeba cells engulf mimivirus particles, fooled by their bacteria-like size and the heavily glycosylated decorating fibrils (La Scola et al., 2003; Raoult et al., 2004; Notaro et al., 2021).
source: Acanthamoeba cells engulf mimivirus particles, fooled by their bacteria-like size and the heavily glycosylated decorating fibrils (La Scola et al., 2003; Raoult et al., 2004; Notaro et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citations to papers describing mimivirus infection mechanism.

claim: The Stargate portal is located at one specific vertex of the mimivirus icosahedron and opens up once in the phagosome (Zauberman et al., 2008).
source: Once in the phagosome, the Stargate portal located at one specific vertex of the icosahedron opens up (Zauberman et al., 2008), enabling the viral membrane to fuse with that of the host vacuole to deliver the nucleoid into the host cytoplasm (Schrad et al., 2020; Claverie et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citation to the paper describing the Stargate structure.

claim: The viral membrane fuses with that of the host vacuole to deliver the nucleoid into the host cytoplasm (Schrad et al., 2020; Claverie et al., 2009).
source: Once in the phagosome, the Stargate portal located at one specific vertex of the icosahedron opens up (Zauberman et al., 2008), enabling the viral membrane to fuse with that of the host vacuole to deliver the nucleoid into the host cytoplasm (Schrad et al., 2020; Claverie et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to papers describing the infection mechanism.

claim: EM studies have shown that the nucleoid gradually loses its electron dense appearance, transcription begins and the early viral factory is formed (Arslan et al., 2011; Suzan-Monti et al., 2007; Mutsafi et al., 2014).
source: EM studies have shown that next the nucleoid gradually loses its electron dense appearance, transcription begins and the early viral factory is formed (Arslan et al., 2011; Suzan-Monti et al., 2007; Mutsafi et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to EM studies of mimivirus infection.

claim: Previous atomic force microscopy studies suggested that the mimivirus DNA forms a highly condensed nucleoprotein complex enclosed within the nucleoid (Kuznetsov et al., 2013).
source: Previous atomic force microscopy studies of the mimivirus infectious cycle suggested that the DNA forms a highly condensed nucleoprotein complex enclosed within the nucleoid (Kuznetsov et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a prior AFM study.

claim: Opening of the large icosahedral capsid in vitro led to the release of rod-shaped structures of about 30-nm width.
source: Here, we show that opening of the large icosahedral capsid in vitro led to the release of rod-shaped structures of about 30-nm width.
evidence: This is directly supported by experimental observations described in the manuscript and shown in figures.

claim: The rod-shaped structures released from opened capsids were characterized using cryo-electron microscopy (cryo-EM), tomography, and mass spectrometry (MS)-based proteomics.
source: These structures were further purified and the various conformations characterized using cryo-electron microscopy (cryo-EM), tomography, and mass spectrometry (MS)-based proteomics.
evidence: This describes the experimental methods used in the study.

claim: An in vitro protocol for particle opening was developed that led to the release of ~30 nm-wide rod-shaped fibers of several microns in length.
source: We developed an in vitro protocol for particle opening that led to the release of ~30 nm-wide rod-shaped fibers of several microns in length (Figure 1, Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by the experimental protocol described and images showing the released fibers.

claim: Complete expulsion of the opened nucleoid content produced bundled fibers resembling a 'ball of yarn' (Kuznetsov et al., 2013; Figure 1C).
source: Complete expulsion of the opened nucleoid content produced bundled fibers resembling a 'ball of yarn' (Kuznetsov et al., 2013; Figure 1C).
evidence: This is supported by citation and by Figure 1C showing the bundled fibers.

claim: The genomic fiber structure becomes completely denatured by heat (95°C) and is sensitive to acidic treatment.
source: The capsid opening procedure involves limited proteolysis and avoids harsh conditions, as we found that the structure becomes completely denatured by heat (95°C) and is also sensitive to acidic treatment, thus preventing its detection in such conditions (Schrad et al., 2020).
evidence: This is based on experimental observations during protocol development.

claim: Various conformations of the genomic fiber were observed, ranging from compact rod-shaped structures to relaxed structures where DNA strands begin to dissociate.
source: Various conformations of the genomic fiber were observed, sometimes even on the same fiber (Figure 1D), ranging from the most compact rod-shaped structures (Figure 1D [left], and Figure 1E, F [top]) to more relaxed structures where DNA strands begin to dissociate (Figure 1D [right], and Figure 1E, F [bottom]).
evidence: This is supported by images showing different conformational states of the fiber.

claim: All opened capsids released genomic fibers.
source: All opened capsids released genomic fibers (Figure 1C, Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental protocol supported by images.

claim: The presence of DNA in the genomic fiber was confirmed by agarose gel electrophoresis.
source: The first confirmation of the presence of DNA in the genomic fiber was obtained by agarose gel electrophoresis (Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claim: Cryo-EM bubblegram analysis indicated that nucleic acid is located in the fiber lumen.
source: Cryo-EM bubblegram analysis (Wu et al., 2012; Cheng et al., 2014) gave a further indication that the nucleic acid is located in the fiber lumen.
evidence: This is based on experimental cryo-EM bubblegram analysis with citations to the method.

claim: The genomic fiber specimen could sustain higher electron irradiation before the appearance of bubbles compared to other studies (Mishyna et al., 2017): 600 e−/Å² for relaxed helices and up to 900 e−/Å² for long compact ones.
source: Surprisingly, the specimen could sustain higher electron irradiation before the appearance of bubbles compared to other studies (Mishyna et al., 2017): 600 e−/Å² for relaxed helices and up to 900 e−/Å² for long compact ones, while no bubbles could be detected in unfolded ribbons (Figure 1—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is based on experimental bubblegram data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 4 and compared to cited literature.

claim: No bubbles could be detected in unfolded ribbons of the genomic fiber.
source: Surprisingly, the specimen could sustain higher electron irradiation before the appearance of bubbles compared to other studies (Mishyna et al., 2017): 600 e−/Å² for relaxed helices and up to 900 e−/Å² for long compact ones, while no bubbles could be detected in unfolded ribbons (Figure 1—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is based on experimental bubblegram data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 4.

claim: Bacteriophage capsids containing free DNA show bubbling for doses of ~30–40 e−/Å² (Mishyna et al., 2017).
source: For comparison, bacteriophage capsids containing free DNA, that is not in the form of nucleoproteins, show bubbling for doses of ~30–40 e−/Å² (Mishyna et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a comparative study.

claim: Three independent clusters (Cl) could be distinguished from 2D classification, corresponding to the compact (Cl1), intermediate (Cl2), and relaxed (Cl3) fiber conformations.
source: Three independent clusters (Cl) could be distinguished, corresponding to the compact (Cl1), intermediate (Cl2), and relaxed (Cl3) fiber conformations (Figure 1—figure supplement 6) with the latter being the widest.
evidence: This is based on computational analysis of cryo-EM data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 6.

claim: After 3D refinement, helical structures of 3.7 Å resolution were obtained for both Cl1a and Cl3a conformations.
source: For both Cl1a and Cl3a conformations, after 3D refinement, we obtained helical structures of 3.7 Å resolution (Fourrier shell correlation [FSC] threshold 0.5, masked), corresponding to 5-start left-handed helices made of a ~8-nm-thick proteinaceous external shell (Figure 2—figure supplements 1–2).
evidence: This is based on cryo-EM 3D reconstruction data shown in supplementary figures.

claim: The Cl1a and Cl3a conformations correspond to 5-start left-handed helices made of a ~8-nm-thick proteinaceous external shell.
source: For both Cl1a and Cl3a conformations, after 3D refinement, we obtained helical structures of 3.7 Å resolution (Fourrier shell correlation [FSC] threshold 0.5, masked), corresponding to 5-start left-handed helices made of a ~8-nm-thick proteinaceous external shell (Figure 2—figure supplements 1–2).
evidence: This is based on cryo-EM 3D reconstruction data.

claim: In the most compact conformation (Cl1a), five dsDNA strands line the interior of the protein shell leaving a ~9-nm-wide central channel.
source: For the most compact conformation (Cl1a) five dsDNA strands were lining the interior of the protein shell leaving a ~9-nm-wide central channel (Figures 2 and 3, Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is based on cryo-EM structural data shown in Figures 2 and 3.

claim: In the relaxed subcluster Cl3a, the DNA strands at the interface to the ~17-nm-wide central channel are not clearly recognizable.
source: In the relaxed subcluster Cl3a, the DNA strands at the interface to the ~17-nm-wide central channel are not clearly recognizable (Figure 2, Supplementary file 1, and Figure 2—figure supplement 2), most likely because they are at least partially detached inside the broken expanded fiber.
evidence: This is based on cryo-EM structural data and interpretation of the relaxed state.

claim: The breaks after relaxation of the helix might be the result of the extraction and purification treatment.
source: The breaks after relaxation of the helix might be the result of the extraction and purification treatment, while DNA will remain in the central channel, at least in the early phase of Acanthamoeba infection.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the observed structural changes.

claim: The 4-Å resolution Cl2 map corresponds to a 6-start left-handed helix made of a ~8-nm-thick proteinaceous external shell.
source: Finally, the 4-Å resolution Cl2 map obtained after 3D refinement (Figure 2—figure supplement 3) corresponds to a 6-start left-handed helix made of a~8-nm-thick proteinaceous external shell, with six dsDNA strands lining the shell interior and leaving a ~12-nm-wide inner channel (Figure 2, Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is based on cryo-EM 3D reconstruction data.

claim: The Cl2 conformation has six dsDNA strands lining the shell interior and leaving a ~12-nm-wide inner channel.
source: Finally, the 4-Å resolution Cl2 map obtained after 3D refinement (Figure 2—figure supplement 3) corresponds to a 6-start left-handed helix made of a~8-nm-thick proteinaceous external shell, with six dsDNA strands lining the shell interior and leaving a ~12-nm-wide inner channel (Figure 2, Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is based on cryo-EM 3D reconstruction data.

claim: MS-based proteomic analyses identified two GMC oxidoreductases as the main components of the purified genomic fiber (qu_946 and qu_143).
source: MS-based proteomic analyses performed on three biological replicates identified two GMC oxidoreductases as the main components of the purified genomic fiber (qu_946 and qu_143 in mimivirus reunion corresponding to L894/93 and R135, respectively, in mimivirus prototype) (Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This is based on mass spectrometry proteomic data from three biological replicates.

claim: The two mimivirus reunion GMC oxidoreductases (qu_946 and qu_143) share 69% identity (81% similarity).
source: The two mimivirus reunion proteins share 69% identity (81% similarity).
evidence: This is based on sequence comparison analysis.

claim: GMC oxidoreductases compose the fibrils surrounding mimivirus capsids (Notaro et al., 2021; Boyer et al., 2011).
source: This is quite unexpected, since GMC oxidoreductases are already known to compose the fibrils surrounding mimivirus capsids (Notaro et al., 2021; Boyer et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: The GMC oxidoreductase genes are highly expressed during the late phase of the infection cycle at the time of virion assembly.
source: The corresponding genes are highly expressed during the late phase of the infection cycle at the time of virion assembly.
evidence: This is based on knowledge of gene expression patterns during mimivirus infection.

claim: The proteomic analyses provided different sequence coverages for the GMC oxidoreductases depending on whether samples were intact virions or purified genomic fiber preparations, with substantial under-representation of the N-terminal domain in the genomic fiber.
source: Notably, the proteomic analyses provided different sequence coverages for the GMC oxidoreductases depending on whether samples were intact virions or purified genomic fiber preparations, with substantial under-representation of the N-terminal domain in the genomic fiber (Figure 2—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is based on proteomic data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 4.

claim: The maturation of the GMC oxidoreductases involved in genome packaging must be mediated by one of the many proteases encoded by the virus or the host cell.
source: Accordingly, the maturation of the GMC oxidoreductases involved in genome packaging must be mediated by one of the many proteases encoded by the virus or the host cell.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed N-terminal truncation in the genomic fiber.

claim: Mimivirus M4 lacks the genes responsible for the synthesis of the two polysaccharides decorating mimivirus fibrils (Boyer et al., 2011).
source: Interestingly, mimivirus M4 (Boyer et al., 2011), a laboratory strain having lost the genes responsible for the synthesis of the two polysaccharides decorating mimivirus fibrils (Notaro et al., 2021) also lacks the GMC-oxidoreductase genes.
evidence: This is supported by citations to papers describing the M4 strain.

claim: Mimivirus M4 also lacks the GMC-oxidoreductase genes.
source: Interestingly, mimivirus M4 (Boyer et al., 2011), a laboratory strain having lost the genes responsible for the synthesis of the two polysaccharides decorating mimivirus fibrils (Notaro et al., 2021) also lacks the GMC-oxidoreductase genes.
evidence: This is based on genomic analysis of the M4 strain.

claim: An additional step of refinement focused on the asymmetric unit improved the local resolution to 3.3 Å.
source: An additional step of refinement focused on the asymmetric unit further improved the local resolution to 3.3 Å as indicated by the corresponding FSC (Figure 3 and Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is based on cryo-EM focused refinement data.

claim: Five additional N-terminal residues in each monomer were manually built using the uninterpreted density available in the Cl1a map.
source: After fitting the most abundant GMC-oxidoreductase qu_946 (SWISS-MODEL model Waterhouse et al., 2018) in the final map of Cl1a, five additional N-terminal residues in each monomer were manually built using the uninterpreted density available.
evidence: This is based on model building using the cryo-EM density map.

claim: The cysteines of each monomer (C51 in qu_946) are close enough to allow a disulfide bridge.
source: This strikingly brings the cysteines of each monomer (C51 in qu_946) close enough to allow a disulfide bridge, directly after the 50 amino acids domain not covered in the proteomic analysis of the genomic fiber (Figure 3G, Figure 2—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is based on structural analysis of the cryo-EM map and model.

claim: The N-terminal chain is absent in the focused refined map and in the Cl3a map of the relaxed helix, suggesting that a break of the disulfide bridge could be involved in the observed unwinding process.
source: The N-terminal chain, being more disordered than the rest of the structure, it is absent in the focused refined map, and also absent in the Cl3a map of the relaxed helix, suggesting that a break of the disulfide bridge could be involved in the observed unwinding process.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation based on structural observations.

claim: In the 3.3-Å resolution map of the asymmetric unit, most side chains and the FAD cofactor are accommodated by density suggesting that the oxidoreductase enzyme could be active.
source: In the 3.3-Å resolution map of the asymmetric unit, most side chains and notably the FAD cofactor are accommodated by density suggesting that the oxidoreductase enzyme could be active (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is based on structural analysis of the high-resolution cryo-EM map and is speculative regarding enzyme activity.

claim: Density that can be attributed to the FAD cofactor is present in the Cl2 and Cl3a maps.
source: Density that can be attributed to the FAD cofactor is also present in the Cl2 and Cl3a maps.
evidence: This is based on analysis of the cryo-EM density maps.

claim: The atomic models of Cl1a and Cl3a dimers are superimposable with a core root-mean-square deviation (RMSD) of 0.68 Å based on Cα atoms.
source: The atomic models of Cl1a and Cl3a dimers are superimposable with a core root-mean-square deviation (RMSD) of 0.68 Å based on Cα atoms.
evidence: This is based on structural comparison of the atomic models.

claim: Inspection of individual genomic fibers in the tomograms confirmed the coexistence of both 5- and 6-start left-handed helices containing DNA.
source: Inspection of individual genomic fibers in the tomograms confirmed the coexistence of both 5- and 6-start left-handed helices containing DNA (Figure 1—figure supplement 2 and Figure 3—animation 1, Figure 1—video 1).
evidence: This is based on cryo-electron tomography data.

claim: In some intermediate and relaxed structures, DNA segments appeared detached from the protein shell and sometimes completely absent from the central channel of the broken fibers.
source: Further, some intermediate and relaxed structures were also observed in which the DNA segments appeared detached from the protein shell and sometimes completely absent from the central channel of the broken fibers.
evidence: This is based on observations from cryo-electron tomography.

claim: Large electron dense structures that might correspond to proteins inside the lumen were sometimes visible in relaxed or broken fibers.
source: In relaxed or broken fibers, large electron dense structures that might correspond to proteins inside the lumen were sometimes visible (Figure 1—figure supplement 2C, E and Figure 1—video 3) as well as dissociating DNA fragments, either in the central channel (Figure 1—figure supplement 2B and Figure 1—video 2) or at the breakage points of the fibers in its periphery (Figure 1—figure supplement 2D and Figure 1—video 4).
evidence: This is based on observations from cryo-electron tomography with speculation about their identity.

claim: Densities corresponding to the dimer subunits composing the protein shell were commonly observed on dissociated DNA strands.
source: Densities corresponding to the dimer subunits composing the protein shell were also commonly observed on dissociated DNA strands (Figure 1E, F, Figure 1—figure supplement 2, and Figure 1—video 1; Figure 1—video 2; Figure 1—video 3; Figure 1—video 4).
evidence: This is based on observations from cryo-electron tomography.

claim: In the Cl1a and Cl2 helices, the monomers in each dimer are interacting with two different dsDNA strands.
source: In the Cl1a and Cl2 helices, the monomers in each dimer are interacting with two different dsDNA strands.
evidence: This is based on structural analysis of the cryo-EM maps.

claim: The DNA strands are interspersed between two dimers, each also corresponding to a different strand of the protein shell helix.
source: As a result, the DNA strands are interspersed between two dimers, each also corresponding to a different strand of the protein shell helix (Figure 3).
evidence: This is based on structural analysis shown in Figure 3.

claim: The interactions between protein shell and DNA strands in the Cl1a helix might involve one aspartate (D82), one glutamate (E321), two lysines (K344, K685), one arginine (R324), and a histidine (H343) in qu_946.
source: Based on the periodic contacts between protein shell and DNA strands, these interactions might involve, in the case of the Cl1a helix, one aspartate (D82 relative to the N-terminal methionine in qu_946), one glutamate (E321), two lysines (K344, K685), one arginine (R324), and a histidine (H343) or one asparagine (N80), two lysines (K319, K342), one arginine (R322), and one tyrosine (Y687), in the case of the qu_143 (Figure 3E, F, Supplementary file 3).
evidence: This is based on structural analysis of protein-DNA contacts in the cryo-EM map.

claim: The interactions between protein shell and DNA strands in the Cl1a helix might involve one asparagine (N80), two lysines (K319, K342), one arginine (R322), and one tyrosine (Y687) in qu_143.
source: Based on the periodic contacts between protein shell and DNA strands, these interactions might involve, in the case of the Cl1a helix, one aspartate (D82 relative to the N-terminal methionine in qu_946), one glutamate (E321), two lysines (K344, K685), one arginine (R324), and a histidine (H343) or one asparagine (N80), two lysines (K319, K342), one arginine (R322), and one tyrosine (Y687), in the case of the qu_143 (Figure 3E, F, Supplementary file 3).
evidence: This is based on structural analysis of protein-DNA contacts in the cryo-EM map.

claim: The mimivirus linear genome of 1.2 × 10^6 bp would extend over ~400 µm and occupy a volume of 1.3 × 10^6 nm^3 in B-form DNA.
source: Assuming that the length of DNA in B-form is ~34 Å for 10 bp, the mimivirus linear genome of 1.2 × 106 bp would extend over ~400 µm and occupy a volume of 1.3 × 106 nm3 (~300 µm and ~1 × 106 nm3 if in A-form) (Li et al., 2019).
evidence: This is a calculation based on known DNA geometry parameters with citation.

claim: The volume of the nucleoid (~340 nm in diameter) is approximately 2.1 × 10^7 nm^3.
source: The volume of the nucleoid (Kuznetsov et al., 2010) (~340 nm in diameter) is approximately 2.1 × 107 nm3 and could accommodate over 12 copies of viral genomes in a naked state, but only 40 µm of the ~30-nm-wide flexible genomic fiber.
evidence: This is a calculation based on the measured nucleoid diameter with citation.

claim: The nucleoid could accommodate over 12 copies of viral genomes in a naked state, but only 40 µm of the ~30-nm-wide flexible genomic fiber.
source: The volume of the nucleoid (Kuznetsov et al., 2010) (~340 nm in diameter) is approximately 2.1 × 107 nm3 and could accommodate over 12 copies of viral genomes in a naked state, but only 40 µm of the ~30-nm-wide flexible genomic fiber.
evidence: This is a calculation based on volume constraints.

claim: The mimivirus genome cannot be simply arranged linearly in the genomic fiber and must undergo further compaction to accommodate the 1.2 Mb genome in a ~40-µm-long genomic fiber.
source: Obviously, the mimivirus genome cannot be simply arranged linearly in the genomic fiber and must undergo further compaction to accommodate the 1.2 Mb genome in a ~40-µm-long genomic fiber.
evidence: This is an inference based on the volume calculations.

claim: The complete mimivirus genome, folded at least five times, fits into the helical shell.
source: As a result, the complete mimivirus genome, folded at least five times, fits into the helical shell.
evidence: This is an inference based on the structural data and volume constraints.

claim: The mimivirus genomic fiber structure resembles the archaea infecting APBV1 nucleocapsid (Ptchelkine et al., 2017).
source: This structure surprisingly resembles a nucleocapsid, such as the archaea infecting APBV1 nucleocapsid (Ptchelkine et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a comparative observation with citation to the APBV1 structure.

claim: The proteomic analysis of fiber preparations revealed the presence of several RNA polymerase subunits: Rpb1 and Rpb2 (qu_530/532 and qu_261/259/257/255), Rpb3/11 (qu_493), Rpb5 (qu_245), RpbN (qu_379), and Rpb9 (qu_219).
source: The proteomic analysis of fiber preparations revealed the presence of additional proteins including several RNA polymerase subunits: Rpb1 and Rpb2 (qu_530/532 and qu_261/259/257/255), Rpb3/11 (qu_493), Rpb5 (qu_245), RpbN (qu_379), and Rpb9 (qu_219), in addition to a kinesin (qu_313), a regulator of chromosome condensation (qu_366), a helicase (qu_572), to be possibly associated with the genome (Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This is based on mass spectrometry proteomic data.

claim: A kinesin (qu_313), a regulator of chromosome condensation (qu_366), and a helicase (qu_572) were identified in the genomic fiber and are possibly associated with the genome.
source: The proteomic analysis of fiber preparations revealed the presence of additional proteins including several RNA polymerase subunits: Rpb1 and Rpb2 (qu_530/532 and qu_261/259/257/255), Rpb3/11 (qu_493), Rpb5 (qu_245), RpbN (qu_379), and Rpb9 (qu_219), in addition to a kinesin (qu_313), a regulator of chromosome condensation (qu_366), a helicase (qu_572), to be possibly associated with the genome (Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This is based on mass spectrometry proteomic data with speculation about their function.

claim: At least three oxidative stress proteins were identified in the genomic fiber in addition to the two GMC oxidoreductases.
source: In addition to the two GMC oxidoreductases, at least three oxidative stress proteins were also identified together with hypothetical proteins (Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This is based on mass spectrometry proteomic data.

claim: RNA polymerase subunits start being expressed 1hr postinfection with a peak after 5 hr and are expressed until the end the infection cycle.
source: RNA polymerase subunits start being expressed 1hr postinfection with a peak after 5 hr and are expressed until the end the infection cycle.
evidence: This is based on knowledge of mimivirus gene expression patterns.

claim: GMC oxidoreductases, kinesin, and regulator of chromosome condensation are all expressed after 5 hr of infection until the end of the cycle.
source: GMC oxidoreductases, kinesin, regulator of chromosome condensation are all expressed after 5 hr of infection until the end of the cycle.
evidence: This is based on knowledge of mimivirus gene expression patterns.

claim: The core protein (qu_431) and major capsid proteins (MCP, qu_446) were significantly decreased in the genomic fiber proteome compared to intact virions.
source: As expected, the core protein (qu_431) composing the nucleoid and the major capsid proteins (MCP, qu_446) were significantly decreased in the genomic fiber proteome compared to intact virions.
evidence: This is based on comparative proteomic analysis.

claim: qu_431 and qu_446 represent 4.5% and 9.4% of the total protein abundance in virions whereas they only account for 0.4% and 0.7% of the total protein abundance in the genomic fiber.
source: In fact, qu_431 and qu_446 represent, respectively, 4.5% and 9.4% of the total protein abundance in virions whereas they only account for 0.4% and 0.7% of the total protein abundance in the genomic fiber, suggesting that they could be contaminants in this preparation.
evidence: This is based on quantitative proteomic analysis.

claim: Enrichment factors of more than 500 (qu_946) and 26 (qu_143) were calculated in the genomic fiber samples compared to the intact virion.
source: On the contrary, we calculated enrichment factors of more than 500 (qu_946) and 26 (qu_143) in the genomic fiber samples compared to the intact virion.
evidence: This is based on quantitative proteomic analysis.

claim: The most abundant RNA polymerase subunit (qu_245) is increased by a factor of eight in the genomic fiber compared to intact virion.
source: Finally, the most abundant RNA polymerase subunit (qu_245) is increased by a factor of eight in the genomic fiber compared to intact virion (if the six different subunits identified are used, the global enrichment is sevenfold).
evidence: This is based on quantitative proteomic analysis.

claim: Macromolecules resembling the characteristic structure of the poxviruses RNA polymerase (Grimm et al., 2019) were frequently observed scattered around the unwinding fiber and sometimes sitting on DNA strands near broken fibers.
source: Furthermore, upon inspection of the negative staining micrographs, macromolecules strikingly resembling the characteristic structure of the poxviruses RNA polymerase (Grimm et al., 2019) were frequently observed scattered around the unwinding fiber and sometimes sitting on DNA strands near broken fibers (Figure 4).
evidence: This is based on negative staining EM observations with comparison to cited poxvirus RNA polymerase structure.

claim: Some RNA polymerase units could occupy the center of the genomic fiber.
source: Together with the tomograms showing large electron dense structures in the lumen, some RNA polymerase units could occupy the center of the genomic fiber.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation based on tomography observations and proteomic data.

claim: The DNA of filamentous viruses infecting archaea is wrapped by proteins to form a ribbon which in turn folds into a helical rod forming a cavity in its lumen (DiMaio et al., 2015; Wang et al., 2020).
source: For instance, the DNA of filamentous viruses infecting archaea is wrapped by proteins to form a ribbon which in turn folds into a helical rod forming a cavity in its lumen (DiMaio et al., 2015; Wang et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies of archaeal virus structures.

claim: The chromatin of cellular eukaryotes consists of DNA wrapped around histone complexes (Robinson et al., 2006).
source: In contrast, the chromatin of cellular eukaryotes consists of DNA wrapped around histone complexes (Robinson et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citation and represents established knowledge.

claim: The virally encoded histone doublets of the Marseilleviridae can form nucleosomes (Liu et al., 2021; Valencia-Sánchez et al., 2021).
source: It was recently shown that the virally encoded histone doublets of the Marseilleviridae can form nucleosomes (Liu et al., 2021; Valencia-Sánchez et al., 2021) and such organization would be consistent with previous evolutionary hypotheses linking giant DNA viruses with the emergence of the eukaryotic nucleus (Bell, 2001; Bell, 2020; Chaikeeratisak et al., 2017; Claverie, 2006; Takemura, 2001).
evidence: This is supported by citations to recent studies.

claim: The nucleosome organization in Marseilleviridae would be consistent with previous evolutionary hypotheses linking giant DNA viruses with the emergence of the eukaryotic nucleus (Bell, 2001; Bell, 2020; Chaikeeratisak et al., 2017; Claverie, 2006; Takemura, 2001).
source: It was recently shown that the virally encoded histone doublets of the Marseilleviridae can form nucleosomes (Liu et al., 2021; Valencia-Sánchez et al., 2021) and such organization would be consistent with previous evolutionary hypotheses linking giant DNA viruses with the emergence of the eukaryotic nucleus (Bell, 2001; Bell, 2020; Chaikeeratisak et al., 2017; Claverie, 2006; Takemura, 2001).
evidence: This is an inference connecting recent findings to evolutionary hypotheses with citations.

claim: Herpesviruses (Gong et al., 2019; Liu et al., 2019), bacteriophages (Sun et al., 2015; Rao and Feiss, 2015), and APBV1 archaeal virus (Ptchelkine et al., 2017) package their dsDNA genome as naked helices or coils.
source: Herpesviruses (Gong et al., 2019; Liu et al., 2019), bacteriophages (Sun et al., 2015; Rao and Feiss, 2015), and APBV1 archaeal virus (Ptchelkine et al., 2017) package their dsDNA genome as naked helices or coils.
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies of various virus structures.

claim: APBV1 nucleocapsid structure strikingly resembles the mimivirus genomic fiber with a proteinaceous shell enclosing the folded dsDNA genome.
source: Yet, APBV1 nucleocapsid structure strikingly resemble the mimivirus genomic fiber with a proteinacious shell enclosing the folded dsDNA genome.
evidence: This is a comparative observation based on structural similarities.

claim: Mimivirus genomic fiber is a nucleocapsid further bundled as a ball of yarn into the nucleoid, itself encased in the large icosahedral capsids.
source: Consequently, mimivirus genomic fiber is a nucleocapsid further bundled as a ball of yarn into the nucleoid, itself encased in the large icosahedral capsids.
evidence: This is a summary interpretation of the structural findings.

claim: The structure of the mimivirus genomic fiber supports a complex assembly process where the DNA must be folded into five or six strands prior to or concomitant with packaging.
source: The structure of the mimivirus genomic fiber described herein supports a complex assembly process where the DNA must be folded into five or six strands prior to or concomitant with packaging, a step that may involve the repeat containing regulator of chromosome condensation (qu_366) identified in the proteomic analysis of the genomic fiber.
evidence: This is an inference based on the structural findings and proteomic data.

claim: The proteinaceous shell, via contacting residues between the dsDNA and the GMC oxidoreductases, would guide the folding of the dsDNA strands into the structure prior loading into the nucleoid.
source: The proteinaceous shell, via contacting residues between the dsDNA and the GMC oxidoreductases, would guide the folding of the dsDNA strands into the structure prior loading into the nucleoid.
evidence: This is a speculative model based on the structural observations.

claim: The lumen of the fiber is large enough to accommodate the mimivirus RNA polymerase.
source: The lumen of the fiber being large enough to accommodate the mimivirus RNA polymerase, we hypothesize that it could be sitting on the highly conserved promoter sequence of early genes (Suhre et al., 2005).
evidence: This is based on size measurements from the cryo-EM structures.

claim: The RNA polymerase could be sitting on the highly conserved promoter sequence of early genes (Suhre et al., 2005).
source: The lumen of the fiber being large enough to accommodate the mimivirus RNA polymerase, we hypothesize that it could be sitting on the highly conserved promoter sequence of early genes (Suhre et al., 2005).
evidence: This is a speculative hypothesis with citation to promoter sequence data.

claim: The central position of RNA polymerase would support its involvement in genome packaging into the nucleoid and could determine the channel width via its anchoring on the genome.
source: This central position would support the involvement of the RNA polymerase in genome packaging into the nucleoid and could determine the channel width via its anchoring on the genome (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is a speculative model based on structural and proteomic findings.

claim: The RNA polymerase could be sterically locked inside the compact form of the genomic fiber and could start moving and transcribing upon helix relaxation.
source: According to this scenario, the available space (although tight) for the RNA polymerase inside the genomic fiber lumen suggests it could be sterically locked inside the compact form of the genomic fiber and could start moving and transcribing upon helix relaxation, initiating the replicative cycle and the establishment of the cytoplasmic viral factory.
evidence: This is a speculative mechanistic model based on structural observations.

claim: The genome and the transcription machinery are compacted together into a proteinaceous shield, ready for transcription upon relaxation.
source: The genome and the transcription machinery would thus be compacted together into a proteinaceous shield, ready for transcription upon relaxation (Figure 2—video 1).
evidence: This is a summary of the proposed model based on the findings.

claim: This organization is conceptually reminiscent of icosahedral and filamentous dsRNA viruses which pack and protect their genomes together with the replicative RNA polymerase into an inner core (Toriyama, 1986; Collier et al., 2016; Ding et al., 2019).
source: This is conceptually reminiscent of icosahedral and filamentous dsRNA viruses which pack and protect their genomes together with the replicative RNA polymerase into an inner core (Toriyama, 1986; Collier et al., 2016; Ding et al., 2019).
evidence: This is a comparative observation with citations to dsRNA virus structures.

claim: In dsRNA viruses, replication and transcription take place within the protein shield and viral genomes remain protected during their entire infectious cycle.
source: As a result, replication and transcription take place within the protein shield and viral genomes remain protected during their entire infectious cycle.
evidence: This is based on knowledge of dsRNA virus biology.

claim: In the case of dsDNA viruses, the double helix must additionally open up to allow transcription to proceed, possibly involving the helicase identified in the proteomic study.
source: In the case of dsDNA viruses however, the double helix must additionally open up to allow transcription to proceed, possibly involving the helicase identified in our proteomic study (Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This is an inference based on knowledge of DNA transcription requirements and the proteomic findings.

claim: The FAD containing GMC oxidoreductases making the proteinaceous shield, together with other oxidative stress proteins, could alleviate the oxidative stress to which the virions are exposed while entering the cell by phagocytosis.
source: Finally, in addition to their structural roles, the FAD containing GMC oxidoreductases making the proteinaceous shield, together with other oxidative stress proteins (Supplementary file 2), could alleviate the oxidative stress to which the virions are exposed while entering the cell by phagocytosis.
evidence: This is a speculative functional hypothesis based on the presence of oxidoreductases and oxidative stress proteins.

claim: Mimivirus virion appears as a Russian doll, with its icosahedral capsids covered with heavily glycosylated fibrils, two internal membranes, and the genomic fiber folded in the nucleoid.
source: Mimivirus virion thus appears as a Russian doll, with its icosahedral capsids covered with heavily glycosylated fibrils, two internal membranes, one lining the capsid shell, the other encasing the nucleoid, in which the genomic fiber is finally folded.
evidence: This is a summary description of the overall virion architecture based on the findings.

claim: The structure of the genomic fiber used by mimivirus to package and protect its genome represents the first description of the genome organization of a giant virus.
source: To our knowledge, the structure of the genomic fiber used by mimivirus to package and protect its genome in the nucleoid represents the first description of the genome organization of a giant virus.
evidence: This is a claim about the novelty of the findings based on knowledge of the field.

claim: The genomic fiber appears to be expelled from the nucleoid as a flexible and subsequently straight structure starting decompaction upon release, suggesting that an active, energy-dependent, process is required to bundle it into the nucleoid during virion assembly.
source: Since the genomic fiber appears to be expelled from the nucleoid as a flexible and subsequently straight structure starting decompaction upon release, we suspect that an active, energy-dependent, process is required to bundle it into the nucleoid during virion assembly.
evidence: This is a speculative inference based on observations of fiber behavior upon release.

claim: The efficient genomic fiber structure is most likely shared by other members of the Mimiviridae family infecting Acanthamoeba.
source: Such an efficient structure is most likely shared by other members of the Mimiviridae family infecting Acanthamoeba and could be used by other dsDNA viruses relying on exclusively cytoplasmic replication like poxviruses to immediately express early genes upon entry into the infected cell (Malkin et al., 2003; Blanc-Mathieu et al., 2021).
evidence: This is a speculative extrapolation based on the findings with citations.

claim: The genomic fiber structure could be used by other dsDNA viruses relying on exclusively cytoplasmic replication like poxviruses to immediately express early genes upon entry into the infected cell (Malkin et al., 2003; Blanc-Mathieu et al., 2021).
source: Such an efficient structure is most likely shared by other members of the Mimiviridae family infecting Acanthamoeba and could be used by other dsDNA viruses relying on exclusively cytoplasmic replication like poxviruses to immediately express early genes upon entry into the infected cell (Malkin et al., 2003; Blanc-Mathieu et al., 2021).
evidence: This is a speculative extrapolation with citations to poxvirus studies.

claim: The parsimonious use of moonlighting GMC oxidoreductases playing a central role in two functionally unrelated substructures of the mimivirus particle questions the evolutionary incentive leading to such an organization for a virus encoding close to a thousand proteins.
source: Finally, the parsimonious use of moonlighting GMC oxidoreductases playing a central role in two functionally unrelated substructures of the mimivirus particle: (1) as a component of the heavily glycosylated peripheral fibril layer and (2) as a proteinaceous shield to package the dsDNA into the genomic fibers questions the evolutionary incentive leading to such an organization for a virus encoding close to a thousand proteins.
evidence: This is an interpretive statement raising an evolutionary question based on the findings.
